ko.text: The library opens with all Must features

name: Library Project
scope: Building renovation, new self-service kiosks, cabling, a mobile app and an online catalog for readers.
intro: You've just taken over the project to modernize the city library. The grand opening is in 12 weeks.
predWorld: Building renovation, kiosk procurement, cabling. Fixed contracts, deadlines and permits. The Gantt chart rules.
agileWorld: Mobile app and online catalog. Requirements evolve, the team works in sprints and gathers feedback.

dependency.hint: Kiosk–catalog integration is waiting for a predictive milestone: kiosk delivery.

workstreams.name: Library building renovation
workstreams.why: The construction has a building permit, a fixed budget and strict sequencing (structure first, then plaster). Changes midway are extremely expensive, so it's planned up front.

workstreams.name: Self-service kiosk procurement
workstreams.why: Public tender: specification, bidding, contract and delivery time. The requirements are clear and the process is set by law.

workstreams.name: Cabling and network infrastructure
workstreams.why: Cables go into the walls at a precise phase of construction. It depends on the construction schedule and can't change later.

workstreams.name: GDPR compliance and security audit
workstreams.why: Regulatory requirements are set by law and need formal documentation and approval by a fixed date.

workstreams.name: Mobile app for readers
workstreams.why: Nobody knows in advance exactly what readers will value. Short iterations and feedback from real users lead to a better product.

workstreams.name: Online catalog and reservations
workstreams.why: Software can be delivered in slices and improved continuously. Features are prioritized by value to readers.

workstreams.name: Kiosk interface design
workstreams.why: Design is best tuned through prototypes and testing with real visitors – and that's iterative work.

workstreams.name: Experiment: AI book recommendations
workstreams.why: High uncertainty: we don't know if it will work. Short-cycle experiments let us learn fast (or stop in time).

milestones.name: Kiosk contract
milestones.okText: The tender finished on time and the contract is signed. The kiosks arrive in sprint 3 and the team can start integrating.
milestones.lateText: The tender dragged on. The kiosks won't arrive until sprint 4 – the agile team has to replan.

milestones.name: Building handover
milestones.okText: The building is handed over on schedule. The library can start moving in.
milestones.lateText: Construction ran late. Contract penalties and an unhappy committee.

milestones.name: Grand opening
milestones.okText: The library opens and every “Must” feature works. Readers reserve books from their phones and the kiosks!
milestones.lateText: The opening happened, but key features are missing:

events.title: The director wants a café
events.text: Midway through the renovation the director has an idea: “There should be a café on the ground floor!” The construction project doesn't account for it at all.
events.lesson: In the predictive part, changes go through formal change control: assess the impact on time, cost and risk, then decide.

choices.text: Order the builders to do it now – the director's the boss
choices.feedback: The director is delighted, but extra work, a new permit and rerouted utilities cost time and money.

choices.text: Start change control: impact analysis and a steering committee decision
choices.feedback: After the analysis, the committee decided the café will come in stage two. The director understands – they saw the numbers.

choices.text: Reject it outright – scope is frozen
choices.feedback: The plan is protected, but the director feels ignored. You can't reject changes without assessing them.

events.title: Librarians want a change after the demo
events.text: At the sprint review, librarians realize reservations should also support “reserve for a whole class” – for teachers. Nobody saw that coming.
events.lesson: In the agile part, change is welcome. The new requirement goes into the backlog and the Product Owner prioritizes it against everything else.

choices.text: Add it to the backlog; the Product Owner orders it by value
choices.feedback: The librarians see the team is listening. Findings like this are exactly why we hold reviews.

choices.text: Reject it – the requirements were clear
choices.feedback: We chose agile precisely so we could react to findings like this. And we just threw that away.

choices.text: Stop the sprint and rework it right away
choices.feedback: Work in progress went to waste and the team is frustrated. A sensible change can wait for the next planning.

events.title: The kiosks are delayed
events.text: The kiosk supplier reports a 3-week production delay. The agile team had planned the kiosk integration.
events.lesson: Dependencies between the predictive and agile parts belong in the risk register. The agile team can work around a delay (simulator, backlog replanning).

choices.text: Draw on the schedule buffer; meanwhile the team develops against a kiosk simulator
choices.feedback: The delay was absorbed. The simulator even caught two bugs before the kiosks arrived.

choices.text: Threaten the supplier with penalties and change nothing
choices.feedback: Penalties recover some money, but the kiosks still arrive late and the team waits.

choices.text: Cancel the kiosks – the app is enough
choices.feedback: The kiosks were a key requirement of the city. The steering committee is unpleasantly surprised.

events.title: The retrospective found a gap
events.text: At the retrospective it turns out the developers don't know when the building network will be ready – so they can't test the kiosks on site.
events.lesson: The interface between the predictive and agile parts needs a shared dependency plan and regular communication.

choices.text: Set up a shared dependency map and a weekly sync with the site manager
choices.feedback: Both teams now see when they're waiting on each other. On-site testing is scheduled.

choices.text: Let the developers figure it out themselves
choices.feedback: Information gets lost and integration keeps slipping.

choices.text: Builders will attend every daily scrum
choices.feedback: Information flows, but it slows the builders down and the daily drags on.

events.title: Budget cut
events.text: The city announces: the project budget is cut by 10%. You have to save somewhere.
events.lesson: The iron triangle (time–cost–scope): in a hybrid project, the usual sacrifice is the agile part's scope (Could features), not quality or safety.

choices.text: Drop the app's “Could” features and defer them to the next stage
choices.feedback: Savings with no impact on key features. MoSCoW paid off.

choices.text: Save on testing
choices.feedback: Money saved today, you'll pay back many times over in post-launch bugs.

choices.text: Cut construction costs with cheaper materials
choices.feedback: Changing materials requires a new assessment and reworked design documentation.

events.title: GDPR audit
events.text: The data protection officer wants proof of how the app processes reader data. It can't launch without approval.
events.lesson: Compliance requirements in the agile part are best handled by adding them to the Definition of Done – then every feature is “done” including documentation.

choices.text: Add GDPR requirements to the Definition of Done
choices.feedback: Every new feature is now compliant from the start. The audit goes smoothly.

choices.text: We'll deal with it at the end of the project
choices.feedback: Retroactive documentation and last-minute fixes are expensive and risky.

choices.text: Halt development for a whole sprint and document everything
choices.feedback: The audit is passed, but at the cost of a lost sprint.

events.title: Key developer is leaving
events.text: The only developer who understands the integration with the old library system has resigned. She has a month left.
events.lesson: A low “bus factor” is a risk. Knowledge sharing (pair programming, documentation) reduces dependence on individuals.

choices.text: Pair programming and knowledge transfer + start hiring
choices.feedback: Next sprint is slower, but the knowledge no longer walks out the door with one person.

choices.text: Change nothing, it'll work out somehow
choices.feedback: After she leaves, nobody knows how the integration works. Bugs pile up.

choices.text: Offer her a raise to stay
choices.feedback: She stayed, but the risk remains – she may leave again next time.

events.title: Builders found asbestos
events.text: Asbestos was found while tearing down a partition wall. Removal will take time and money. This risk was in the risk register.
events.lesson: Identified risks should have a prepared response and a reserve. Well-separated project parts let the agile team keep going even when construction hits trouble.

choices.text: Activate the risk reserve and adjust the construction schedule; development continues
choices.feedback: The risk response plan worked. The committee appreciates that the project was prepared.

choices.text: Stop the whole project, development included, until it's resolved
choices.feedback: App development has nothing to do with asbestos. Time wasted for nothing.

choices.text: Keep quiet and carry on
choices.feedback: Health inspectors shut the site down and the story hit the news. A major loss of trust.

choices.text: Negotiate emergency money with the sponsor and replan
choices.feedback: With no reserve ready, you have to find money and get a new plan approved. It costs time and trust.
